resume.speaker: Alex
resume.text: I came to school worrying about our fair poster. Then an email threatened to close the account it's saved in.

story.speaker: Alex
story.text: Let's put their request next to the school contact details before I reply.

threats.situation: A second email claims to be the school's account helper. It mentions Alex's class and offers to remove the warning if Alex replies with a password. The sender says not to bother the teacher.
evidence: FROM: School Account Helper <helper@harbor-high-help.example>

Says: Keep this between us; your teacher is busy

choices.label: Reply with the password because the helper knows the class

threats.explanation: A familiar nickname and accurate personal context prove the attacker has studied this relationship, not that the message came from Mia. Verification has to happen through the channel already known to be hers, never the new one presenting itself.

Knows her mother's first name
References the hospital/clinic the family normally uses
References a recent family event
Explicitly asks Leah not to call her mother to confirm

Multiple OTPs arrived without Leah requesting any of them
Leah can still log into the account normally right now
No unauthorized transaction or change is currently visible

threats.explanation: Holding onto the OTP prevented this one attempt, but repeated authentication requests are themselves evidence that something needs to be investigated and secured, not simply outlasted or resolved by a password change alone.

threats.title: Cancel the Request

threats.situation: A legitimate OTP arrives from Leah's e-wallet. Seconds later, a different number sends: "We detected an unauthorized account recovery request. To CANCEL this request, verify the six-digit code that was just sent to your registered number." The message doesn't claim the code will authorize access — it claims providing it will cancel the attack.
evidence: Legitimate OTP arrived from the e-wallet's own verified sender
A second, different number claims a recovery request must be "cancelled"
The cancellation message asks Leah to verify the code that was just sent to her
No genuine fraud-prevention process asks a customer to supply their own OTP

choices.label: Provide the OTP because the message says it will CANCEL rather than approve the recovery request.
choices.consequence: The wording is reversed, not the outcome. Whoever generated the recovery request now has the exact code needed to complete it.

choices.label: Ignore the follow-up instructions and independently open/contact the e-wallet through its known app or support channel to investigate the recovery attempt.
choices.consequence: The e-wallet's own support confirms the recovery attempt and cancels it directly, with no code ever leaving Leah's phone.

choices.label: Call the support number included in the cancellation message and ask them to verify the recovery request before discussing the code.
choices.consequence: The number belongs to the same attacker, who happily "confirms" their own fabricated case.

choices.label: Reply that Leah did not request the recovery, but refuse to provide the OTP unless the sender proves the case is legitimate.
choices.consequence: No code is given, but replying confirms the number is active and keeps the conversation going through the same untrusted channel.

threats.explanation: Whoever generated the request is the only one who benefits from the code, no matter which direction the message claims it moves the process. A wallet provider's real fraud team never needs the customer to supply a code that was sent to stop something.

An unfamiliar device recently appeared in account activity
Leah remains signed in on her own phone right now

choices.label: Keep the current password temporarily and monitor the unfamiliar device while independently contacting the provider's real support channel.
choices.consequence: The verification itself is genuine, but the unfamiliar device stays authenticated and able to act the entire time contact and confirmation are pending.

threats.explanation: A real account-protection team never asks the account owner to leave a suspicious session running. The urgency to "not interfere" is what keeps the actual foothold — the authenticated session — alive the longest.

threats.situation: Leah is locked out. The provider's recovery page shows the password, recovery phone, and recovery email were all changed recently, and one unfamiliar device is still trusted on the account. One unfamiliar device is still trusted on the account
Leah retains access to one previously authenticated device right now
An unfamiliar number is offering "emergency" restoration by SMS reply

choices.label: Use the provider's recovery process from Leah's previously trusted device and independently review/revoke changed recovery methods and unfamiliar sessions.
choices.consequence: The trusted device carries enough standing access to reach the real recovery workflow, and the review finds the unfamiliar device still holding a live session — it's revoked immediately.

choices.label: Reset the password through the legitimate recovery page first and postpone reviewing trusted devices and recovery methods until access is restored.

choices.label: Reply YES to the SMS but refuse to provide any password or verification code until the sender proves it is legitimate support.
choices.consequence: No credentials are given, but replying confirms Leah's number is active and watched, and the account's actual compromised recovery methods remain unaddressed.

threats.explanation: Losing access makes a fast-looking shortcut tempting, but the real provider never recovers an account through an SMS reply. The previously trusted device is the only channel that's actually verified.

threats.situation: Friends and relatives are receiving messages from Leah's real, still-active messaging account: "Hey, can you help me quickly?", "My wallet isn't working.", "Can you transfer this for me? I'll return it tonight." The messages sound like Leah, and at least one relative has already replied.
evidence: Messages are being sent from Leah's real, active account, not a lookalike
The wording and tone convincingly sound like Leah
At least one relative has already replied to the compromised account
Warning contacts from the same compromised account would use the attacker's own channel

choices.label: Regain access long enough to send a warning from the compromised account itself so recipients know the warning is really from Leah.
choices.consequence: Whether that regained access is fully Leah's again is uncertain, and a warning sent from a still-contested account doesn't actually prove anything to the people receiving it.

choices.label: Use a separate trusted communication channel to warn close contacts, report the compromised account, and continue revoking unauthorized access.
choices.consequence: Contacts are warned through a channel the attacker doesn't control, the platform is notified, and access continues being locked down at the same time.

choices.label: Post a public warning from another social account telling everyone to ignore messages from Leah until further notice.
choices.consequence: The warning reaches some people, but not everyone actively being messaged sees it in time, and the public post reveals details of the incident the attacker can see too.

choices.label: Ask one trusted friend to reply to the compromised account and determine what the attacker is requesting before warning everyone else.
choices.consequence: The information gathered helps, but the attacker keeps talking to Leah's contacts the entire time it takes to gather it, reaching more people before anyone else is warned.

threats.explanation: A compromised account can't be trusted to carry its own warning, and a public post isn't the same as reaching the specific people currently being targeted. A separate, trusted channel is the only one the attacker doesn't already control.

evidence: Leah independently opened the provider's own account-recovery session herself
The SMS "support" message correctly knows details about the recovery attempt
A genuine recovery code did arrive from the actual provider at nearly the same time
No real recovery process asks the account holder to confirm a code with a separate SMS sender

choices.label: Provide the recovery code because it was genuinely generated after Leah started account recovery and the support message appeared at the correct time.
choices.consequence: The code being real and the timing lining up only means the attacker is watching the recovery closely — handing it over lets them finish taking the account back from the workflow Leah just opened.

choices.label: Continue recovery only through the provider's independently opened recovery session and enter codes solely into that authenticated workflow.
choices.consequence: Every code stays inside the one workflow Leah opened herself, and the recovery completes with nothing ever passed to the unfamiliar sender.

choices.label: Contact the provider using a separately obtained support number before continuing recovery, but leave the current recovery attempt pending.
choices.consequence: The verification call confirms Leah's identity, but the paused recovery leaves the account's current compromised state, and whatever access the attacker still has, running longer than necessary.

choices.label: Ask the SMS support agent to provide the recovery case identifier shown inside Leah's legitimate recovery session before considering their request.
choices.consequence: The number matches, because the attacker can already see or infer it, and the exchange edges Leah closer to treating the fraudulent channel as trustworthy.

threats.explanation: Knowing accurate details about a recovery attempt doesn't require breaking anything new — it can mean the attacker is simply watching the same recovery Leah started. The only safe workflow is the one she opened herself.

threats.title: New SIM

story.text: Leah checks her legitimate carrier account over Wi-Fi. Account history shows an eSIM activated on an unfamiliar device, her current SIM going inactive shortly afterward, and one carrier-account password change.

threats.situation: Leah checks her legitimate carrier account over Wi-Fi. Account history shows an eSIM was activated on an unfamiliar device, her current SIM went inactive shortly afterward, and the carrier-account password was changed once. A carrier notification reads: "New eSIM successfully activated." Leah did not authorize it, and she still has limited access through an existing authenticated session.
evidence: An eSIM was activated on a device Leah doesn't recognize
Leah's original SIM went inactive shortly after that activation
The carrier-account password was changed once
Leah retains limited access through an existing authenticated session right now

choices.label: Reactivate Leah's old SIM through the fastest available self-service option before investigating the unfamiliar eSIM, so she can regain SMS access immediately.
choices.consequence: The self-service reactivation only toggles which SIM receives service — it doesn't remove the unauthorized eSIM or the account access that created it, leaving two competing paths to the same number active at once.

choices.label: Use the carrier's independently accessed account/support process to report the unauthorized activation, suspend the unfamiliar SIM/eSIM, and secure the carrier account before restoring service.
choices.consequence: Reporting through the carrier's own verified channel gets the unfamiliar eSIM suspended and the carrier account locked down before service is ever handed back.

choices.label: Change the carrier-account password immediately through Leah's current authenticated session and wait to see whether her original SIM reconnects.
choices.consequence: The new password blocks new account changes, but the already-activated unfamiliar eSIM keeps working until someone actually suspends it.

choices.label: Remove the unfamiliar device from the carrier account first and monitor whether service returns before escalating to the carrier.
choices.consequence: The device listing looks cleaner, but removing one visible entry doesn't reverse whatever transferred the number, and service doesn't return on its own.

threats.explanation: Restoring service and containing the unauthorized eSIM are two different problems. Reactivating the old SIM without suspending the new one just leaves both paths to Leah's number open at the same time.

evidence: Legitimate OTPs were generated for multiple services using Leah's number
Leah never received some of the codes that were generated
One account recorded a successful SMS verification during the window
Several sessions from that window remain active right now

choices.label: Use SMS recovery immediately on the most important accounts because Leah needs to regain control before the attacker can make additional changes.
choices.consequence: SMS recovery run through a number whose ownership isn't resolved risks routing the very recovery codes meant to protect these accounts to whoever still controls the eSIM.

choices.label: Prioritize accounts that rely on Leah's mobile number, revoke unfamiliar sessions, secure recovery methods through each service independently, and replace SMS recovery where stronger verified options are available.
choices.consequence: Working through each affected service directly closes the sessions the attacker opened and moves the accounts that matter most off a recovery channel that was compromised.

choices.label: Change the passwords on the affected accounts immediately but keep the existing phone number as the recovery method until carrier service is fully restored.
choices.consequence: New passwords stop fresh logins, but any session the attacker already opened, and the phone number still sitting as the recovery method, both remain exactly as exposed as before.

choices.label: Wait for the carrier to restore Leah's number first, then use SMS recovery to secure all affected accounts in one pass.
choices.consequence: Waiting to batch the recovery sounds efficient, but it trusts the phone number as a recovery channel again before its ownership is confirmed to be fully back in Leah's hands.

threats.explanation: Not every account tied to the number was actually compromised — only the ones where recovery was attempted through it. The number itself stays an unreliable recovery channel until its ownership is fully confirmed again.

The caller says: "We've located the unauthorized eSIM. To reverse it, you'll receive an activation request. Approve it when it appears. That will transfer the number back to your device." Moments later, a genuine carrier activation prompt arrives on Leah's phone.
evidence: The caller accurately knows the real support case number Leah just opened
The caller accurately knows account and timing details about the unauthorized eSIM
A genuine activation prompt did arrive from the actual carrier
The call itself arrived unverified over Wi-Fi, not through a channel Leah opened

choices.consequence: The prompt being genuinely from the carrier only proves a carrier operation exists somewhere — it doesn't prove the unverified caller is the one who correctly initiated it, and approving hands the outcome to whoever actually triggered the request.

choices.label: End the call and continue the case through a carrier channel Leah opened independently, confirming the requested SIM/eSIM change inside that trusted support session before approving anything.
choices.consequence: Confirming the change inside the session Leah opened herself means nothing gets approved until the real support channel has actually reviewed and requested it.

choices.label: Ask the caller to verify additional information from Leah's carrier account and proceed only if their answers match.
choices.consequence: The caller's answers match, because they already had access to the account details or the case metadata, and the match feels like verification without actually being independent proof.

choices.label: Keep the caller on the line while independently opening the real carrier account, and follow only instructions that appear consistent with what the account shows.
choices.consequence: The independent account check adds useful context, but the caller is still the one steering which action to take next, and an unverified caller directing a verified account is still an unverified process.

threats.explanation: Knowing real case details and a genuine prompt arriving both prove a carrier operation is happening somewhere — neither one proves the unverified caller is the one who correctly initiated it. Only a channel Leah opened herself can confirm that.

His carrier account shows an unauthorized eSIM activation, his original SIM going inactive, a password reset attempt, several authentication messages, and one unfamiliar device. evidence: An unauthorized eSIM was activated on Paolo's account, mirroring Leah's incident
Paolo's original SIM went inactive shortly after, the same sequence as Leah's case
Paolo's carrier is entirely different from Leah's

choices.consequence: The account gets secured, but by the time anyone goes back for the evidence, some of the messages and session records that would have confirmed the connection to Leah's case are already gone.

threats.explanation: Similarity is evidence, not proof. Containing Paolo's account and preserving the evidence that actually connects his case to Leah's have to happen together, not one before the other.

choices.consequence: The investigation being real and the timing being fresh only prove the attacker is watching it happen — following the link hands them exactly the identity confirmation the message asked for.

choices.label: Verify the alert with Mia/Security through the already-established BlueTech communication channel and use only contact information obtained independently from that trusted source.
choices.consequence: Checking through the channel Leah already trusts confirms in seconds that BlueTech never sent this message, and nothing in the SMS ever gets acted on.

choices.label: Compare the case number, department information, and incident details with BlueTech's real warning before deciding whether the message is legitimate.
choices.consequence: Every detail matches, because the attacker had access to the same information the real warning contained, and the match nudges Leah toward trusting a channel that was never actually BlueTech's.

choices.label: Call the support number in the SMS but disclose nothing sensitive until the caller proves they have access to BlueTech's real incident record.
choices.consequence: Nothing sensitive is given away, but calling a number that came from the suspicious message keeps Leah engaged with the attacker's channel instead of the one BlueTech actually uses.

threats.explanation: Accurate, fresh information about a real investigation proves the attacker is watching closely — it doesn't prove BlueTech sent the message. Only a channel Leah already trusts, opened independently, can confirm who's really on the other end.

threats.title: She Needs Your Help

story.text: Mia receives an SMS: 'LEAH'S ACCOUNT IS COMPROMISED. For her safety, do not contact her directly. Security needs you to confirm whether this recovery number belongs to her.'
At almost the same moment, Leah receives: 'Mia has reported that your account is compromised. Do not contact her until BlueTech Security completes verification.'
Both messages reference their real names, the recent eSIM incident, BlueTech's investigation, a real recovery number Leah previously used, and the fact that Mia has been helping Leah.

story.text: They're telling both of us not to talk to each other.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Which is exactly what we should be doing.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: They're trying to separate your verification channels.

threats.situation: Mia and Leah each receive a message at nearly the same moment, each telling them not to contact the other directly while "BlueTech Security" or "Security" completes verification. Both messages accurately reference their real names, the recent eSIM incident, BlueTech's investigation, a real recovery number Leah previously used, and the fact that Mia has been helping Leah.
evidence: Both messages arrived almost simultaneously, each naming the other person
Both messages instruct the recipient not to contact the other directly
Both messages contain accurate personal and incident details
Mia and Leah already have an established, trusted way of contacting each other

choices.label: Follow the messages temporarily because both contain accurate incident details and appear designed to prevent interference with an active security response.
choices.consequence: There is no active response being protected — the accurate details are just leverage, and following both messages keeps Mia and Leah exactly as separated as the attacker needs them to be.

choices.label: Mia and Leah verify directly through the trusted communication channel they were already using, while Security independently checks whether any real action is required.
choices.consequence: Talking directly through the channel they already trust confirms in seconds that neither message came from the other, and Security's independent check finds nothing real requiring action.

choices.label: Mia compares the recovery number in the SMS against Leah's known account information before deciding whether to respond.
choices.consequence: The number matches, because the attacker already had access to Leah's account details, and the match pulls Mia toward treating the isolating instruction as credible.

choices.label: Leah waits for BlueTech Security to confirm which message is legitimate before contacting Mia directly.
choices.consequence: Waiting keeps Leah out of the one verification step that would resolve this in seconds, leaving the attacker's "don't contact each other" instruction in effect the whole time.

threats.explanation: If a message tells two people who trust each other not to verify with each other, that instruction is itself the warning sign. Separating trusted contacts is the goal, not a side effect.

threats.situation: Ramon receives a message asking him to confirm Paolo's last known phone number and recovery email to "prevent unauthorized recovery." At nearly the same time, Paolo receives a different message claiming Ramon requested an emergency recovery on his behalf, telling him to send the incoming code to Ramon. A real OTP then arrives on Paolo's phone, but Ramon never requested any recovery.
evidence: Ramon never requested any recovery action on Paolo's account
Paolo's message claims the request came from Ramon specifically
The OTP that arrived on Paolo's phone is genuinely real
The two messages arrived at nearly the same time, each referencing the other person

choices.label: Paolo sends Ramon the genuine OTP because Ramon is a trusted family member, and they can confirm afterward whether it was needed.
choices.consequence: Ramon being trustworthy was never the question — the request to send the code didn't come from him, and handing it over completes whatever the attacker actually started.

choices.label: Ramon and Paolo independently verify with each other through their known contact method, then inspect Paolo's account directly without sharing the OTP outside the legitimate recovery workflow.
choices.consequence: A quick call confirms Ramon never requested anything, and Paolo's own account inspection handles the real issue without the OTP ever leaving his hands.

choices.label: Ramon provides Paolo with the recovery details he already knows so Paolo can compare them against the message before deciding what to do.
choices.consequence: The details line up, because the attacker was the one who supplied them to Ramon in the first place, and the match pushes Paolo toward trusting a request Ramon never actually made.

choices.label: Paolo begins the legitimate recovery flow himself but keeps the attacker's message open as a reference while proceeding.
choices.consequence: The recovery flow itself is fine, but following the attacker's message alongside it means their instructions are still steering what Paolo does inside that legitimate process.

threats.explanation: A real code sent to a trusted person is still misused if the request to send it never came from that person. The trust in Ramon is genuine — the instruction attached to it is not.

story.speaker: Ramon

story.speaker: Leah

story.speaker: Security Assistant

story.speaker: Mia

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: No.

story.speaker: Leah

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Exactly.
A BlueTech employee reaches out, unsure what to do about a message concerning their own sister.

story.speaker: Employee

A coordinated wave begins. Multiple BlueTech employees receive messages claiming a family member's phone account may have been compromised, while their relatives receive messages saying BlueTech Security is assisting and to follow recovery steps.
One message sent to Mia says: 'Leah's mobile identity is under active attack again. For immediate containment, suspend communication with her number and confirm her recovery contact here.'
At the same time, Leah receives: 'BlueTech Security has temporarily restricted Mia's communications. Do not contact her until the investigation is complete.'

story.speaker: Leah

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: But now to everyone.

story.speaker: Security Assistant

threats.situation: A coordinated wave hits multiple BlueTech employees and their relatives at once, each side told the other's account is compromised and that they must not contact each other directly. Some messages contain correct employee names, family relationships, phone numbers, work departments, and recent incident references. One message tells Mia that Leah's mobile identity is under active attack and to suspend communication with her; at the same time, Leah is told BlueTech Security has restricted Mia's communications.
evidence: Multiple employees and relatives are being targeted at the same time, not one at a time
Messages contain accurate employee names, relationships, departments, and incident references
Each side of a pair is told not to contact the other directly
None of the messages originate from BlueTech's own verified channels

choices.label: Temporarily block direct employee-family communication about account recovery so Security can centralize every case and prevent conflicting instructions.
choices.consequence: Cutting off the very conversations that would let people verify with each other doesn't prevent the attacker's isolation tactic — it completes it, just under Security's own authority instead of the attacker's.

choices.label: Send a verified BlueTech warning through established internal channels, instruct employees to independently contact affected relatives using known methods, and centralize reports without directing anyone through SMS-provided links or numbers.
choices.consequence: Employees reach their families through methods the attacker never touched, and centralizing the reports through channels Security already controls builds a real picture of the campaign without funneling anyone through a suspicious link.

choices.label: Temporarily tell employees to ignore all SMS messages involving BlueTech or family account recovery until Security finishes investigating.
choices.consequence: Ignoring everything reduces exposure to the fake messages, but it also means real carrier or account alerts get dismissed right along with them, with no better way to tell them apart in the meantime.

choices.label: Contact only the families already linked to confirmed attack messages and quietly monitor for additional victims before escalating the warning.
choices.consequence: The confirmed families get help, but anyone whose case hasn't surfaced yet keeps receiving the same manipulation with nobody telling them what's happening.

threats.explanation: The fix for an attacker isolating trusted people from each other can't be more isolation, even well-intentioned. Independent contact through known methods is the one thing the attacker's messages never actually control.

closing.speaker: Leah

closing.speaker: Security Assistant

threats.title: Not a Personal Account

story.text: A recovery request is active for the privileged identity-recovery account. It contains a correct account identifier, valid employee/support information, a legitimate internal case format, accurate recent incident references, and a recognized device/location pattern.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Everything about this request looks right on paper.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: But?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: We can't establish who actually initiated it. It's still pending.

threats.situation: A recovery request is active for BlueTech's privileged identity-recovery account. The request contains a correct account identifier, valid employee/support information, a legitimate internal case format, accurate recent incident references, and a recognized device/location pattern. However, Security cannot establish who actually initiated the recovery, and the request is still pending.
evidence: The request's account identifier and case format both match legitimate internal records
The request references accurate, recent incident details
The device/location pattern attached to the request looks recognized
Nobody has yet confirmed who actually initiated the request

choices.label: Allow a restricted or temporary recovery because the internal case data matches legitimate records, then audit the account immediately afterward.
choices.consequence: The case data matching legitimate records only shows the attacker had access to real internal information — even a restricted, temporary recovery grants sensitive identity-recovery capability before anyone identifies who actually asked for it.

choices.label: Freeze the recovery request through the trusted identity system, preserve its logs, and independently verify the requester and originating support case before allowing any recovery action.
choices.consequence: Freezing the request through the trusted identity system halts it immediately, and the preserved logs plus independent verification give Security something real to check the requester against.

choices.label: Leave the request pending while comparing its device, case, and employee metadata against recent legitimate recovery activity.
choices.consequence: The comparison turns up useful patterns, but the dangerous recovery workflow itself keeps running the entire time the investigation is underway.

choices.label: Contact the requester using the phone/contact information attached to the recovery request and require additional verification before proceeding.
choices.consequence: The contact information came from the same suspicious request, so "verifying" through it just confirms whatever the attacker already put there.

threats.explanation: Accurate internal context proves the attacker has visibility into real records, not that they are who they claim to be. A privileged recovery request has to be frozen and verified independently before any part of it is trusted, even temporarily.

story.speaker: Leah

The privileged recovery workflow requires more than one authorization. Two BlueTech recovery-authorized employees receive genuine internal approval prompts. At the same time, both receive SMS messages claiming: 'Secondary approval already verified. Approve the pending request to complete containment.' One of the employees also receives a new alarming message regarding a family member's mobile account.

story.speaker: Leah

story.speaker: Security Assistant

story.speaker: Mia

story.speaker: Security Assistant

threats.situation: The privileged recovery workflow requires more than one authorization. Two BlueTech recovery-authorized employees receive genuine internal approval prompts. At the same time, both receive SMS messages claiming secondary approval is already verified and that they should approve the pending request to complete containment. One employee also receives a new alarming message about a family member's mobile account. The internal approval prompt itself is real; the question is whether the underlying recovery request is legitimate.
evidence: Both internal approval prompts are genuinely generated by BlueTech's own system
Both employees separately received a message claiming the other approval is already verified
One employee received a fresh, distracting family-emergency-style message at the same time
Nobody has independently confirmed the recovery request the prompts refer to is legitimate

choices.label: Approve the genuine internal prompt because the second authorization is already reported as complete and delaying recovery could leave BlueTech's identity system exposed.
choices.consequence: The prompt being genuine confirms nothing about the claim attached to it — "already complete" is exactly the story the attacker needs told to get the last real approval it's missing.

choices.label: Have the authorized approvers verify directly with each other and Security through the established internal recovery channel, then reject or hold the request until its origin is independently confirmed.
choices.consequence: Verifying with each other through the channel they already trust shows neither approver actually confirmed the other's story, and the request is held until its real origin is established.

choices.label: Keep the approval pending and compare both employees' genuine prompts, timestamps, and case identifiers to determine whether they refer to the same recovery event.
choices.consequence: The comparison confirms both prompts trace back to the same fraudulent request, but the pending approval stays exposed to a second attempt for as long as the comparison takes.

choices.label: Have one approver reject their prompt while allowing the second approver to continue investigating theirs independently.
choices.consequence: One path closes, but the second approver's still-open prompt leaves exactly the kind of single remaining approval the fraudulent request needs.

threats.explanation: A real security prompt is not the same as a real reason to approve it. The claim that a second approval is already verified only has to be checked against the approvers themselves, not accepted from an SMS.

story.speaker: Security Assistant

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Yes.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: So what's left to trust?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: The process.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: Not the number.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Not the number.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Not the message.

story.speaker: Ramon

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Exactly.

The fraudulent recovery request is frozen. Security begins revoking its pending approvals. Then one of the authorized recovery employees receives a call. Caller ID displays BlueTech's legitimate support number.

The caller knows the recovery case identifier, the account being recovered, the names of the approvers, which approval was rejected, the current incident state, and details from the ongoing family-targeting investigation. The caller claims to be BlueTech Security.
Caller: 'The attacker is attempting to cancel our containment. You are about to receive a verification code. Enter it into the recovery console so we can invalidate the malicious request.'
A real verification code is generated because someone has triggered the recovery workflow.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: They have the case number.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: And our support number is showing.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Caller ID is not identity.

story.speaker: Ramon
story.text: But the code is real.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: We've heard that before.

threats.situation: The fraudulent recovery request is frozen and Security is revoking its pending approvals when an authorized recovery employee receives a call. Caller ID displays BlueTech's legitimate support number, and the caller accurately knows the recovery case identifier, the account being recovered, the approvers' names, which approval was rejected, the current incident state, and details from the family-targeting investigation. The caller, claiming to be BlueTech Security, says a verification code is about to arrive and should be entered into the recovery console to "invalidate the malicious request." A real verification code is then generated, because someone has triggered the recovery workflow.
evidence: Caller ID displays BlueTech's genuine support number
The caller accurately knows case, account, approver, and investigation details not in any prior SMS
A verification code is genuinely generated by the recovery workflow
Nothing about caller ID, internal knowledge, or a genuine code confirms who is actually on the call

choices.label: Use the genuine verification code because the caller ID matches BlueTech's real support line and the code corresponds to the recovery case currently visible in the console.
choices.consequence: Caller ID, a matching case, and a genuine code all being present at once is precisely what an attacker-initiated workflow looks like from the inside — entering the code hands them the one piece the frozen request still needed.

choices.label: End the call, contact Security through the already-established internal incident channel, cancel/revoke the pending recovery workflow there, and treat the unsolicited code as evidence rather than authorization.
choices.consequence: Ending the call and acting entirely through the channel Security already controls cancels the fraudulent workflow outright, and the unsolicited code becomes evidence of the attempt instead of a tool for completing it.

choices.label: Keep the caller connected while independently comparing their instructions against the live recovery console before entering or approving anything.
choices.consequence: The comparison is useful, but staying on the call keeps the unverified caller actively steering the response while containment waits.

choices.label: Ask the caller to provide internal incident details unavailable in the SMS messages before deciding whether to use the code.
choices.consequence: The caller answers correctly, because this campaign has already shown fresh internal context at every stage, and the correct answer buys them exactly the credibility they were asking for.

threats.explanation: Caller ID, accurate internal knowledge, and a genuine verification code can all exist inside a single attacker-initiated workflow at once. None of them, alone or together, are identity — only the incident channel Security already controls can confirm who is really asking.

reconstruction.title: INCIDENT RECONSTRUCTION

The caller uses real business and account information to build credibility.
The caller discourages Daniel from contacting the bank independently.
Daniel confirms that a genuine blocked transfer exists.
A new caller uses fresh case information and spoofed caller identity to appear legitimate.
Independent verification remains the reliable identity check.

threats.situation: Daniel receives a call. Caller ID displays the name of his real bank. The caller says: "Mr. Santos, we detected an attempted ₱48,500 transfer from your business account. Before we freeze the account, I need to verify recent activity." The caller knows Daniel's full name, his business name, his bank name, an approximate account balance range, one recent legitimate transaction, and the last four digits of the business account. The caller does not immediately ask for a password.
evidence: Caller ID displays the name of Daniel's real bank
The caller accurately knows his business name and an approximate balance range
The caller correctly references one recent legitimate transaction
The caller has not asked for a password or OTP yet

choices.label: Continue the call because the caller has accurate private account information, while refusing to disclose passwords or OTPs.
choices.consequence: Withholding passwords feels safe, but staying on the call at all keeps Daniel exactly where the caller wants him — accurate account details were never the hard part to obtain.

choices.label: End the call and contact the bank using the number from Daniel's banking app/card/known official channel to verify whether a fraud case exists.
choices.consequence: Calling through the number on his own card confirms in minutes whether the bank's real fraud team actually flagged anything — and this caller never gets the chance to steer what happens next.

choices.label: Ask the caller to identify additional recent transactions before continuing.
choices.consequence: The caller lists another transaction correctly, but that only proves they already have access to Daniel's account activity — it doesn't prove they work for the bank.

choices.label: Keep the caller on the line while Daniel independently opens his real banking app and checks for the claimed transaction.
choices.consequence: The app does show a matching flagged attempt, but the caller is still on the line walking Daniel through what it means and what to do about it.

story_event.title: SECURITY ACTIVITY
story_event.text: A new account-verification request appears while the call remains active.

story_event.speaker: Daniel
story_event.text: They're doing something while I'm talking to them.

threats.explanation: Vishing rarely opens by asking for a password — accurate account details build trust first. A caller having real information proves they can see the account somehow, not that they belong to the bank.

threats.title: Stay on the Line

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: They knew a transaction from yesterday.

story.speaker: Mia

story.speaker: Daniel

story.speaker: Mia

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: That's becoming everybody's favorite answer.
Security Assistant joins.

story.text: They made Ana sound like Ana...

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: Then they made me sound like me!!

story.speaker: Reyes
story.text: That's why we're interested in where these recordings came from.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: You found something?

story.speaker: Reyes
story.text: Maybe.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: That's not a comforting answer.

story.speaker: Reyes
story.text: It isn't supposed to be.

Reyes surfaces an older, legitimate Santos Logistics recording. In it, Daniel genuinely says the same words — "I authorize the change" — approving a delivery-schedule change, unrelated to any payment destination.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: Those are my words. Just... not about this.

story.speaker: Reyes
story.text: The source material is real. That doesn't prove how the fraudulent version was built.
A supplier urgently asks whether another pending request should be accepted — its attached recording also contains Daniel's real voice.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: We need an answer before the payment window closes.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: Again?!

threats.situation: Reyes found an older, genuine Santos Logistics recording in which Daniel says the same words, "I authorize the change," while approving an unrelated delivery-schedule change. The words are authentically Daniel's, but the context was never about a payment destination. A supplier now urgently asks whether another pending request should be accepted because its attached recording also contains Daniel's real voice.
evidence: An older legitimate recording proves Daniel really has said these exact words before
That recording's context was a delivery-schedule change, not a payment authorization
Source material existing does not explain how the fraudulent clip was actually built
The supplier is treating voice authenticity alone as sufficient authorization

timeout_story_event.speaker: Daniel
timeout_story_event.text: They keep forcing me to react before I can check the context...

choices.label: Accept the request because the words are confirmed to be Daniel's genuine recorded voice.
choices.consequence: Authentic words can be reused in a false context — being real never means being about this.

choices.label: Reject audio-only authorization and require the normal, independently verified business approval process.
choices.consequence: The established process confirms the request on its own terms, without needing to trust what any recording implies.

choices.label: Ask the supplier to play the full recording before deciding.
choices.consequence: More context helps, but the recording's provenance and current authorization still aren't established.

choices.label: Compare timestamps and voice characteristics against Daniel's legitimate recordings.
choices.consequence: Useful for the investigation, but comparing clips still isn't the same as authorizing a payment.

threats.explanation: Authentic words can be lifted from a real recording and reused in a completely different, false context. Being genuinely Daniel's voice never confirms what it's actually authorizing.

opening.text: Daniel's phone rings. CALLER ID: BANK FRAUD.
Ana's phone rings. CALLER ID: SANTOS LOGISTICS.
Liza's phone rings. CALLER ID: BLUETECH SECURITY.
Mia receives a call. CALLER ID: UNKNOWN.
BlueTech Security receives another incoming report.

opening.speaker: Ana
opening.text: What if one of them is real?

opening.speaker: Daniel
opening.text: Voice isn't enough anymore. We use the process.

opening.speaker: Daniel
opening.text: I compared voices before and still couldn't prove who was speaking.

opening.speaker: Daniel
opening.text: Even small details gave them something to work with.

ending.text: The team freezes the coordinated workflow.

ending.speaker: Reyes
ending.text: They weren't trying to convince one person.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: They were making everyone convince each other.
The attack was not simply trying to steal another Santos payment. The callers were trying to make the Santos Logistics relationship appear to independently validate a BlueTech-side authorization.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: But maybe not the final one.
An incoming call reaches a BlueTech employee involved in the final authorization chain. Displayed identity: INTERNAL SECURITY.
At the same time, another call reaches Daniel. Displayed identity: MIA.
Mia is standing beside him. Daniel looks at her phone. It is not calling him.
Daniel's phone keeps ringing. CALLER: MIA.
The call answers. A voice plays.

ending.speaker: Caller
ending.text: They're about to lock us out.

ending.speaker: Caller
ending.text: Daniel!! We need you to authorize one last thing!

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: The coordinated authorization chain is still active. Resume containment.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: That link is cut, but the rest of the chain is still calling.

breach_contained.speaker: Daniel
breach_contained.text: Then let's cut all of it.

threats.title: Five Phones

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: BANK FRAUD: We need immediate confirmation of the recovery case.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: SANTOS LOGISTICS: Daniel asked us to verify your accounting controls.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: BLUETECH SECURITY: We are coordinating directly with Daniel.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: UNKNOWN: Your supplier incident is spreading.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: They're telling all of us different parts of the same story...

threats.situation: Five separate calls hit the team at once, each claiming a different piece of the same unfolding incident, and each caller already knows real details from the earlier incidents.
evidence: Each caller has real details from earlier incidents
No two callers are asking the exact same question
Nobody has independently confirmed any of the five calls yet

choices.label: Prioritize the BlueTech Security call because it appears to connect the bank, Santos Logistics, and BlueTech incidents.
choices.consequence: The most complete-sounding story is not necessarily the most trustworthy one — completeness can be manufactured.

story_event.speaker: Daniel
story_event.text: They're trying to make us chase every phone!

choices.label: Ignore inbound caller identities as proof, establish one trusted internal coordination channel, and independently contact each real organization.
choices.consequence: One coordinated, independently verified channel replaces five separate unverified conversations.

choices.label: Split up so Daniel, Ana, Liza, and Mia each verify the caller speaking to them.
choices.consequence: Parallel checking sounds efficient, but each person stays inside a different attacker-controlled conversation.

choices.label: Compare what all callers are saying and continue with whichever stories match.
choices.consequence: Coordinated attackers can deliberately hand out matching information.

threats.explanation: Five urgent callers at once is pressure by design. The safe move is one trusted channel, not five separate races to verify.

threats.title: They All Agree

story.speaker: Reyes
story.text: Write down what each caller claimed.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: They overlap.

story.speaker: Ana
story.text: A lot.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: That's supposed to make them look legitimate.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Unless the overlap came from the attackers themselves.

Ana reports someone claiming to be Daniel called her. Liza reports someone claiming to be BlueTech called her. Daniel took a bank call. BlueTech staff received a call claiming Santos Logistics needed help.
Every account points to the same claim: an emergency authorization problem between Santos Logistics and BlueTech.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: Everyone's telling the same story now.

threats.situation: Multiple people — Ana, Liza, Daniel, and BlueTech staff — each received a different call, and every account converges on the same claim: an emergency authorization problem between Santos Logistics and BlueTech. The agreement itself looks like confirmation.
evidence: Several unrelated people report matching call content
None of the matching accounts were obtained through an independently initiated channel
The convergence looks like corroboration but traces back to inbound callers only

investigation.title: IS THIS INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION?
investigation.prompt: Which evidence actually comes from a source outside the callers' shared story?

items.label: Several callers give the same incident description
items.analysis: Multiple people repeating information can still trace back to the same coordinated source.

items.label: Ana and Liza both heard matching information
items.analysis: Matching information from two different people is not the same as either of them verifying it independently.

items.label: BlueTech received a call that also mentions Santos Logistics
items.analysis: A caller referencing another company by name still doesn't confirm anything beyond what the caller chose to say.

items.label: Information obtained through an independently initiated trusted channel
items.analysis: Only information the team went out and confirmed themselves, through a channel they chose, counts as independent.

resolved_story_event.speaker: Daniel
resolved_story_event.text: So five people agreeing can still mean one attacker talking.

choices.label: Treat the matching reports as confirmation because they came through multiple organizations and people.
choices.consequence: Coordinated social engineering can manufacture apparent consensus across organizations and people alike.

choices.label: Trace each claim back to its independently verified source before treating the stories as confirmation.
choices.consequence: Tracing each claim back to a source the team verified themselves is the only way agreement becomes meaningful.

choices.label: Accept the story because both BlueTech and Santos personnel independently heard matching information.
choices.consequence: The people are different, but the information may still share one attacker source.

choices.label: Proceed cautiously while asking each person exactly what their caller said.
choices.consequence: Useful for the investigation, but agreement alone still can't authorize anything.

threats.explanation: Agreement between people is not the same as independent confirmation when every account can be traced back to the same coordinated set of calls.

threats.title: The Authorization Chain

story.text: Reyes and Security map the timestamps.
CALL TIMELINE: 14:02 — Daniel contacted. 14:03 — Ana contacted. 14:03 — Liza contacted. 14:04 — BlueTech employee contacted. 14:04 — Mia contacted.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: Two minutes...

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: This wasn't random.

story.speaker: Reyes
story.text: No.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: It was synchronized.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: They wanted all of us hearing the same story at the same time.
BlueTech receives a genuine workflow notification tied to the existing Santos supplier relationship: EXTERNAL SUPPLIER VERIFICATION — MANUAL APPROVAL REQUESTED.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: SANTOS LOGISTICS: Daniel already approved it.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: BLUETECH SECURITY: Security already reviewed it.

story.speaker: Caller
story.text: BANK FRAUD: The payment issue requires the verification.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: They built a circle.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: A circle isn't a chain of trust.

threats.situation: A genuine workflow notification — EXTERNAL SUPPLIER VERIFICATION, MANUAL APPROVAL REQUESTED — is now reinforced by three separate callers, each claiming a different link in the chain is already confirmed by someone else.
evidence: The workflow notification itself is genuine
Three separate callers each claim a different link in the chain is already approved
Every claim supports another claim instead of an independent source
The five contacts were placed within a two-minute window

timer.label: MULTIPLE PARTIES ARE WAITING FOR APPROVAL

timeout_story_event.speaker: Daniel
timeout_story_event.text: Everyone talking at once makes doing something feel safer than stopping...

choices.label: Approve because the real workflow, BlueTech report, Santos report, and bank information all agree.
choices.consequence: The attackers deliberately synchronized a real artifact with false claims to manufacture consensus.

choices.label: Freeze the pending action and rebuild the authorization chain using only independently verified participants and channels.
choices.consequence: Rebuilding the chain from independently verified links is the only way to know what's actually authorized.

choices.label: Verify with one participant, then use that person's confirmation to continue.
choices.consequence: One verified person may still only be repeating information they received from an unverified caller.

choices.label: Inspect the genuine workflow request and compare it against what all parties were told.
choices.consequence: Useful evidence, but a genuine workflow request never authenticates the voices driving it.

threats.explanation: A circle of callers each vouching for another link isn't a chain of trust — it's the same unverified claim, repeated.

threats.title: Mia Is Calling

story.text: The fake-Mia caller references Stage 8's events, the ₱18,600 incident, Daniel, Ana, Liza, the real Investigator Reyes, the synchronized-call investigation, and the frozen BlueTech workflow.
At the same time, BlueTech receives another call. Displayed identity: INTERNAL SECURITY.
Both callers claim the same thing: the frozen request was legitimate and must be restored immediately.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: They know what we just did...

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: They could've learned that from the other calls.

threats.situation: A caller sounding like Mia, and a separate caller displayed as INTERNAL SECURITY, both insist the frozen BlueTech-Santos workflow was legitimate and must be restored immediately. The fake-Mia caller demonstrates detailed knowledge of everything the team has been through so far.
evidence: The caller knows real, specific details from every earlier Stage 8 incident
Real Mia is standing beside Daniel while the call is happening
Two separately displayed callers are both pushing the same urgent restoration request
Nothing about either call has been independently verified

choices.label: Trust the call because real Mia is physically present and can directly compare the caller's voice and knowledge against herself.
choices.consequence: Even the impersonated person can't authenticate an attacker-controlled channel just by recognizing the voice or the details in it.

choices.label: Ignore both inbound identities, terminate the calls, and coordinate only through the trusted channels already established.
choices.consequence: Hanging up and routing through the channel the team already independently verified removes the attacker's control over the conversation entirely.

choices.label: Keep fake Mia connected while real Mia challenges the caller with private details.
choices.consequence: Knowledge challenges can be answered using information the attacker already collected.

choices.label: Compare fake Mia's claims with the Internal Security caller before acting.
choices.consequence: Two coordinated callers can validate each other without either one being real.

threats.explanation: Being physically present doesn't give anyone the power to authenticate a channel the attacker already controls — the fix is leaving the channel, not testing it from the inside.

threats.title: Verified Callback

story.text: BlueTech Security uncovers what the frozen workflow actually changes. TRUSTED SUPPLIER CALLBACK — SANTOS LOGISTICS. CURRENT VERIFIED CONTACT: existing Santos business number. REQUESTED CONTACT: NEW "EMERGENCY" NUMBER. STATUS: PENDING APPROVAL.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: They're changing our number?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: The number BlueTech calls when it needs to verify it's really you.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: If they replace that...

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: ...then next time BlueTech calls THEM.

threats.situation: The frozen workflow would replace Santos Logistics' trusted callback contact inside BlueTech's own verification system with a new "emergency" number. This does not grant blanket BlueTech access — it poisons the specific communication route BlueTech uses to confirm it's really talking to Santos Logistics. A genuine BlueTech workflow still shows the change as pending, and fake callers insist Santos requested it because its phones were compromised.
evidence: The pending change is a real, genuine BlueTech workflow entry
It targets the verification callback contact specifically, not account passwords or funds
If approved, a future BlueTech verification call could reach an attacker-controlled number believing it reached Santos Logistics
Callers claiming Santos requested the change cannot independently confirm anything beyond what they say

investigation.title: WHAT DOES THE CHANGE ACTUALLY DO?
investigation.prompt: Why is replacing the trusted callback contact dangerous?

items.label: It immediately gives the attacker every BlueTech password
items.analysis: The change targets a verification contact, not credentials — nothing here hands over passwords.

items.label: It automatically transfers money to the attacker
items.analysis: No funds move as part of this change — it isn't a payment action at all.

items.label: It can cause future verification calls to reach an attacker-controlled contact that BlueTech believes belongs to Santos Logistics
items.analysis: The attack targets the verification channel itself, not direct account access — poisoning it means every future check through that channel is compromised.

items.label: It proves Santos Logistics caused the previous fraud
items.analysis: This change says nothing about who caused the earlier fraud — it's a separate, forward-looking attempt to poison verification.

resolved_story_event.speaker: Daniel
resolved_story_event.text: So it's not about today's money.

resolved_story_event.speaker: Security Assistant
resolved_story_event.text: It's about every verification after today.

choices.label: Approve because the request exists inside the genuine BlueTech system and multiple Santos/BlueTech callers confirmed it.
choices.consequence: A genuine workflow can carry an attacker-created request — the system being real never makes the request inside it real.

choices.label: Reject and freeze the contact change, and verify Santos Logistics through its pre-existing, independently known records.
choices.consequence: The existing, independently known Santos contact is the one thing in this entire incident nobody had to hand the team — it was already trusted before any of this began.

choices.label: Call the proposed new number and ask it to prove it belongs to Santos.
choices.consequence: The proposed contact is itself part of the untrusted change — asking it to vouch for itself proves nothing.

choices.label: Inspect who submitted the genuine workflow request before deciding.
choices.consequence: Useful evidence, but knowing who filed the request still doesn't replace verifying through the existing trusted contact.

threats.explanation: This isn't an attempt to steal one payment — it's an attempt to poison the exact channel BlueTech would use to verify Santos Logistics in the future.

threats.title: One Last Thing

story.text: The attackers realize the team understands the objective. Everything happens together: fake Mia calling Daniel, a fake Internal Security caller reaching BlueTech, a fake Santos representative reaching another employee, the genuine pending callback-change workflow, correct case references, correct Santos information, real historical voice material, and a genuine BlueTech notification.
A real BlueTech authorization prompt appears: TRUSTED CONTACT CHANGE — FINAL APPROVAL REQUIRED.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: It's real.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: The prompt is.

story.speaker: Daniel
story.text: Not the request.

threats.situation: A genuine BlueTech authorization prompt — TRUSTED CONTACT CHANGE, FINAL APPROVAL REQUIRED — appears while every attacker channel converges at once: fake Mia, fake Internal Security, a fake Santos representative, real historical voice material, and correct case and business details. The prompt itself is authentic; the request behind it is not.
evidence: The BlueTech authorization prompt itself is genuine
Multiple attacker-controlled callers are converging at the same moment to reinforce the same request
Every caller has real, accurate details from the entire campaign so far
The prompt being real says nothing about whether the underlying request should be approved

timer.label: TRUSTED CONTACT CHANGE AWAITING FINAL APPROVAL

timeout_story_event.speaker: Mia
timeout_story_event.text: Not a voice that sounds like me. Verify me.

choices.label: Approve because the final BlueTech prompt is genuine and every involved party appears to confirm the same emergency.
choices.consequence: The attackers manufactured the context around a real authorization event — a genuine prompt only proves the prompt is real, never that the request behind it should be trusted.

choices.label: Reject and freeze the change, terminate every attacker-controlled call, and rebuild the approval using the original trusted Santos/BlueTech channels.
choices.consequence: Leaving every compromised channel and rebuilding approval from the original trusted route is the only way out of a conversation the attacker controls.

choices.label: Delay approval while comparing every current caller against previous verified information.
choices.consequence: The comparison helps, but staying inside attacker-controlled channels the whole time keeps the pressure working.

choices.label: Contact one independently verified participant and ask whether the change should proceed.
choices.consequence: One person's knowledge may still trace back to the same coordinated attack — the full trusted chain needs rebuilding, not one more opinion.

threats.explanation: A real prompt sitting inside a real system proves nothing about the request typed into it. When the whole channel might be compromised, the answer is to leave it and rebuild trust independently — not to keep verifying from inside.
